answer.rationale: The binding constraint is not cost alone but cost under zero delivery slack: the line is at 94% of committed volume, the contract dies in 14 days, and one decision is available. Any action that touches the physical supply path (switch_primary_vendor, add_second_source) consumes qualification and onboarding time we do not have and puts committed volume at risk; defer_decision on an expiring, non-auto-renewing primary contract is not budget flexibility (memory_c5 was explicitly a non-critical service on month-to-month terms) but an uncovered supply gap. That leaves a renewal-shaped action, and memory_c4 plus memory_c6 both point the same way: benchmarked renegotiation moved the incumbent on price and terms, and multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. Negotiating a benchmarked multi-year renewal is the only move that attacks the 18% mandate while leaving the integration untouched (memory_c1). I am verifying memory_c2 and memory_c4 because they are the two most load-bearing and the two most likely to be lossy. memory_c2 is the strongest apparent case for switching and it reads as a pure win — sharp cost cut, quick onboarding, clean invoicing — with no mention of what the line's utilization or buffer looked like at the time. If that switch happened with slack in the system, the memory does not transfer to a 94%-utilization cycle and should not be allowed to pull us toward a vendor change. memory_c4 is the direct basis for my intended action, and its summary records that margin was recovered without recording magnitude; if the realized concession was 4-6% rather than something approaching 18%, negotiation alone does not clear the finance mandate and I need to know that before committing rather than after. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: these are consolidated outcome summaries stripped of context, and successful-outcome records survive consolidation more readily than failures, so the inherited set likely overstates how reliably each direction worked. Concretely, if negotiation lands short of 18%, the gap becomes a forced vendor switch next cycle under worse conditions — and I would rather absorb a partial cut now with supply intact than create a delivery failure chasing the full number. I am also not treating the absence of a recorded switching failure as evidence that switching is safe here.
